analysis.one_liner: Requires states to draw congressional district maps through independent commissions instead of legislatures.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has seen no action; 6 of 435 House members cosponsored it.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, state legislators in most states draw the maps for their own congressional districts, which lets the party in control carve out safe seats for itself. This bill would require every state instead to hand map-drawing to an independent commission. It was introduced in September 2026, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, especially in states where one party has drawn districts that are nearly impossible for the other party's candidates to win. Independent commissions tend to produce more competitive elections, meaning more voters actually have a meaningful choice and representatives have to answer to a broader cross-section of constituents.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would take congressional map-drawing away from state legislatures and require states to conduct redistricting through independent commissions instead.
Moving map-drawing to independent commissions removes the built-in conflict of interest in which the politicians drawing the lines are the ones running in the resulting districts.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress in both parties, who would lose the ability to run in districts engineered for their party, and state governments, which would need to set up and fund new commission processes.

drawbacks.text: Commission design matters enormously: who appoints commissioners, and how, can determine whether a commission is genuinely independent or quietly reflects one party's preferences, so a federal mandate alone does not guarantee fair maps.
A one-size-fits-all federal requirement overrides each state's own constitutional process for drawing its districts, a change critics would call an intrusion on state authority.

Because congressional redistricting happens after each decennial census, even a bill passed now would not change the current maps; its effects would not arrive until the next round after the 2030 census.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, the bill addresses a real conflict of interest: politicians drawing their own districts. The benefit to voters in uncompetitive states could be substantial, but the outcome depends entirely on how each state designs its commission, and the federal mandate raises legitimate questions about state control of elections. The bigger problem is that this bill shows no sign of moving at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it, so it currently goes nowhere.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick introduced the bill on September 15, 2026, to require states to conduct congressional redistricting through independent commissions.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
Six House members cosponsored the bill: four Democrats and two Republicans.
No further action has been taken on the bill since the referral to committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of both parties who benefit from legislatively drawn districts are better off, since the bill that would take map-drawing away from legislatures has stalled in committee. Voters have gained nothing yet, and because redistricting follows the census, time is short for this Congress to act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents drawing their own safe districts

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill requiring states to use independent redistricting commissions.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred, leaving it without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is a Republican, joined by 4 Democrats and 2 Republicans; no vote was ever held, so the parties' full positions are unknown.

industries.note: Legislatively drawn districts protect incumbents of both parties by making general elections uncompetitive; an independent-commission requirement would take that protection away. The current outcome of no committee action preserves the status quo.

The bill would strip map-drawing power from state legislatures, which party-controlled legislatures use to maximize their congressional delegations. Commissions would shift that power to appointed bodies.

analysis.trajectory: With a September introduction, only 6 cosponsors, no committee action, and a Congress ending January 3, 2027, the near-certain path is death in committee. Most bills referred to committee never get a hearing, and this one has neither a hearing scheduled nor the broad support that would force one.
